# 0. Executive doctrine

Valtum Studio is not being built to look like a competent local web agency.

The target is a **top-tier Australian software studio with global creative and engineering credibility**: a studio whose public work can sit credibly beside strong US and European digital-product studios, creative-technology studios, product-design firms, award-winning web studios and software-development partners.

That requires two standards to coexist:

1. **World-class authored digital craft** — composition, typography, media, storytelling, motion, interaction, responsive design, originality and visual identity.
2. **World-class software discipline** — product truth, engineering architecture, accessibility, performance, maintainability, QA, backend integrity, data accuracy, task usability and measurable business value.

Valtum must never become an “Awwwards-looking agency” that can only make marketing websites.

It must also never become a generic software consultancy whose website is a white page filled with icon cards and interchangeable corporate language.

The studio's competitive visual position is the intersection:

> **serious software engineering + serious product thinking + serious visual authorship + serious frontend craft.**

The five portfolio products are evidence that Valtum can work across radically different software problems. The flagship Valtum website must make that breadth feel intentional without forcing every product into one house template.

- operational workflows;
- transactions;
- data interpretation;
- education;
- AI-assisted systems;
- analytics;
- computer vision;
- mobile/product UX;

A viewer should not conclude that Valtum is a “web-design-only” company.

A viewer should also not conclude that Valtum is a commodity development outsourcing shop.

# 2. Global studio positioning — Australia as origin, world as market

Valtum is Australia-based, but its design and engineering benchmark is global.

## 2.1 What “Australia-based” should mean visually and commercially

It can communicate:

- a real operating jurisdiction;
- credible business identity;
- professional accountability;
- timezone/communication clarity;
- connection to the Australian technology/design market;
- an internationally understandable point of origin.

It must **not** become:

- kangaroo/country symbolism;
- Australian visual clichés;
- an “Australia only” market position;
- a Darwin-first/local-agency aesthetic;
- small-local-business copy;
- “cheap offshore development with an Australian wrapper.”

## 2.2 Global target

The site and case studies must be comfortable speaking to clients in:

- Australia;
- United States;
- Europe;
- Middle East;
- Asia-Pacific;
- other international markets.

This changes design expectations.

The work needs to survive comparison with:

- US digital product agencies;
- European creative-tech studios;
- award-winning web-design studios;
- specialist interaction-development firms;
- high-end software product studios.

## 2.3 Premium global signals

Premium does not mean dark backgrounds and expensive words.

It means:

- direct positioning;
- strong work above the fold or immediately after;
- credible case studies;
- real software depth;
- evidence of thinking;
- a design system with taste;
- precise copy;
- strong mobile;
- high performance;
- accessible behavior;
- transparent contact;
- confident but bounded claims;
- visible ability to take a problem from strategy to launch.

# 3. 2026 studio benchmark research — United States, Europe and Australia

This section is a fresh research layer completed on 18 August 2026 using current official studio websites/case studies where available, plus recognized award-platform criteria. It does not replace the historical forensic archive; it upgrades the strategic benchmark for Valtum.

The purpose is not to copy any studio.

The purpose is to reconstruct the **operating principles of high-end studios**.

## 3.1 Work & Co — product seriousness + design/technology parity

**Current official positioning:** “We solve complex problems through design & technology.”

Work & Co is useful to Valtum because it behaves more like a digital-product company than a conventional advertising agency.

### Documented signals

- Design and technology are presented together, not as separate vendors.
- Leadership includes senior partners across design, technology, product management, strategy and motion.
- Public leadership material describes significant partner involvement and strong senior talent.
- Multiple leaders are described as hands-on designers or technologists.
- Their work spans architecture through launch, mobile, responsive systems and enterprise products.
- Rapid prototyping and pragmatic product design appear repeatedly in leadership biographies.
- Their current site promotes “The New Model of Software Delivery,” reinforcing that software delivery itself is part of the brand.

### Valtum transfer

**Senior ownership must be real and visible.**

Valtum should not present itself as:

> strategy team → sales handoff → anonymous implementation.

The user has already defined the operating model correctly:

- ChatGPT/design authority performs senior architecture, research, UI/UX, visual direction, motion and frontend design reasoning.
- Coding agents implement explicit contracts.
- Product/backend truth is verified from the repository.

That is closer to a senior-led product studio than to commodity outsourcing.

### Practical doctrine

For Valtum:

- senior design/architecture review is mandatory on every flagship build;
- design and engineering reviews happen together;
- prototypes are used to answer risk, not just impress;
- architecture choices are part of experience design;
- case studies explain pivotal technical decisions, not only final screenshots.

### Do not copy

- Work & Co's site structure;
- brand;
- client language;
- visual identity;
- corporate scale claims.

**Source:** https://work.co/

## 3.2 Instrument — brand, product and marketing as one digital system

Instrument currently describes itself as a digital-first design agency where creativity meets technology and states that it makes **brands, products, websites and campaigns**.

### Documented signals

- Brand, product and marketing are treated as connected surfaces.
- Strategy, creative and technology are integrated.
- Current product work includes mobile applications, design systems and consumer/enterprise products.
- Their Iru case explicitly describes the website as an extension of the platform's brand promise.
- Campaign, website, product and visual identity are designed to reinforce the same story.
- Instrument says it does not merely design; it builds.

### Valtum transfer

Valtum should not separate:

- brand identity;
- marketing website;
- product UX;
- software implementation

into four unrelated visual conversations.

A strong Valtum engagement should aim for **brand-to-interface continuity**.

That does not mean every product looks like its marketing site.

It means the same conceptual identity is translated appropriately into:

- marketing;
- onboarding;
- app/task UI;
- transactional moments;
- dashboards;
- emails/notifications;
- case-study proof.

### Do not copy

- Instrument's visual identity;
- campaign style;
- current client portfolio language.

**Source:** https://www.instrument.com/

## 3.3 ustwo — human-centered product design + deep engineering

ustwo currently positions itself as a **digital product studio** that designs and builds digital experiences with human-centered design and deep technical expertise.

### Documented signals

- Full-stack cross-functional teams can take ideas from discovery to launch.
- Their public approach uses a make/test/learn model.
- They work across full-stack web, native iOS/Android, cross-platform mobile and QA.
- Their engineering practice emphasizes accessibility, build pipelines and architecture as much as visual quality.
- Recent engineering writing advocates an **HTML-first** accessibility approach before unnecessary ARIA or external abstractions.
- Their accessibility practice includes keyboard and screen-reader testing, not just automated contrast checking.
- Long-term partnerships show continuous discovery/delivery, not only one-off handover.

### Valtum transfer

This is especially important because Valtum wants to be a software studio, not a decorative-site studio.

The brain therefore treats:

- accessibility;
- testing;
- architecture;
- release quality;
- maintainability;
- real mobile behavior

as part of UI/UX quality.

### Engineering doctrine

Use native semantics first.

If a `<button>`, `<a>`, `<details>`, `<dialog>`, input or other native element solves the behavior correctly, do not build a custom div-based imitation.

Creative frontend sophistication is layered on top of a semantic foundation.

### Do not copy

- ustwo's visual surface;
- “Play Thinking” branding;
- service-package language.

**Sources:**  
https://ustwo.com/  
https://engineering.ustwo.com/

## 3.4 AREA 17 — research → system → technology → measurable outcomes

AREA 17 is a particularly important benchmark because its public case studies repeatedly connect:

- research;
- experience strategy;
- prototyping;
- design systems;
- technology strategy;
- custom application/interface development;
- analytics/optimization.

### Documented implementation evidence

AREA 17 publicly documents multiple technology patterns:

- Saint Laurent: **headless architecture with React frontend + Salesforce Commerce Cloud backend**.
- Multiple editorial/institutional projects: **Twill**, AREA 17's open-source CMS for Laravel.
- The New School case includes **cloud-native DevOps**.
- TTP/Rockwell and others list custom application development, custom interface development, systems integration and analytics.

### Strategic lesson

Top-tier design does not require one universal stack.

Architecture follows:

- content model;
- commerce;
- editor workflow;
- longevity;
- operational scale;
- integration needs.

### Valtum transfer

Do not turn Next.js/React/Docker/Postgres into brand attributes.

Clients buy:

- maintainability;
- speed;
- ownership;
- capability;
- performance;
- scale;
- useful experiences.

The technology choice should become visible in the case study only when it explains a meaningful design/business decision.

### Do not copy

- AREA 17's CMS choices automatically;
- visual layouts;
- case-study surfaces.

**Source:** https://area17.com/

# 4. Cross-studio synthesis — what the best studios have in common

Across Work & Co, Instrument, ustwo, AREA 17, Clay, Dogstudio, Lusion, Unseen, Locomotive, Bürocratik, Refokus, Build in Amsterdam, Nightjar and Active Theory, the surface styles differ wildly.

The deeper operating patterns converge.

## 4.1 Seniority is part of the product

High-end clients buy judgment.

The studio should expose:

- senior ownership;
- senior review;
- product thinking;
- technical thinking;
- clear decision responsibility.

## 4.2 Design and technology are not sequential vendors

The strongest model is not:

> designers finish → developers reproduce.

It is:

> concept ↔ prototype ↔ architecture ↔ design ↔ engineering ↔ browser refinement.

## 4.3 One discipline does not carry the whole experience

Great work may require:

- UX;
- visual design;
- motion;
- content;
- product strategy;
- frontend;
- backend;
- 3D;
- sound;
- data;
- QA;
- research.

The composition should not be expected to compensate for weak copy, weak engineering or weak assets.

## 4.4 Case studies are commercial proof

The portfolio is not a gallery.

Strong case studies answer:

- What was wrong?
- Why did it matter?
- What did the team decide?
- What did the product need to do?
- What was designed?
- What was built?
- What changed?
- What proof exists?
- What was learned?

## 4.5 Systems are invisible infrastructure, not visible sameness

Top studios use design systems.

But the user should not feel:

> “all six sites use the same component library.”

The system creates:

- consistency;
- accessibility;
- implementation speed;
- maintainability.

Art direction creates:

- identity;
- composition;
- project-specific world;
- narrative.

## 4.6 R&D is useful when attached to client value

A studio can maintain:

- motion experiments;
- shader research;
- interaction prototypes;
- AI workflow experiments;
- mobile patterns;
- accessibility patterns.

But labs must not become an excuse for production gimmicks.

## 4.7 Performance is part of perceived craft

A beautiful experience that:

- stutters;
- hides content;
- blocks for a loader;
- breaks on mobile;
- fails without WebGL

is not premium.

## 4.8 Accessibility is not “after design”

Semantic HTML, keyboard access, screen-reader behavior, reduced motion and target sizing are design constraints from the beginning.

## 4.9 Client ownership matters

CMS, design system, documentation, maintainability, APIs, deployment and analytics affect whether the work remains valuable after launch.

## 4.10 Business outcomes strengthen creative credibility

When legitimate outcomes exist, use them.

Do not invent them.

The strongest studios often show:

- conversion lift;
- engagement;
- adoption;
- reduced friction;
- launch speed;
- accessibility;
- scalability;
- operational efficiency.

# 5. Award-level benchmark — what “9+” means

Valtum should not chase awards by imitating award sites.

Awards are useful because their criteria reveal what high-level reviewers notice.

## 5.1 Awwwards

Public Awwwards scoring pages use the familiar weighting:

- Design — 40%
- Usability — 30%
- Creativity — 20%
- Content — 10%

Developer recognition separately exposes categories such as:

- web-performance optimization;
- responsive design;
- semantics/SEO;
- markup/metadata;
- animation/transitions;
- accessibility.

### Internal lesson

A project cannot reach the target through visuals alone.

But it also cannot reach it through functional correctness alone.

---

## 5.2 Webby 2025/2026 criteria

The Webby Awards' current criteria for websites/mobile include:

- Content;
- Structure & Navigation;
- Visual Design;
- Functionality;
- Interactivity;
- Innovation;
- Overall Experience.

Their current guidance makes a useful point:

> strong interactivity lets the user give and receive; it is more than rollover decoration.

Their “Innovation” framing also asks whether an idea is genuinely new or only another iteration on an existing execution.

### Valtum interpretation

A hover effect is not innovation.

A WebGL model is not innovation.

A product-native interaction that materially changes understanding may be.

**Source:** https://www.webbyawards.com/judging-criteria/

---

## 5.3 CSS Design Awards

CSSDA explicitly separates:

- UI;
- UX;
- Innovation.

Its public FAQ describes UI as interface/aesthetics/effects, UX as experience/functionality and Innovation as new development/design ideas.

### Valtum interpretation

The internal 9+ target must be balanced across:

- visual craft;
- actual usability;
- original execution.

**Source:** https://www.cssdesignawards.com/

# 6. Valtum internal 100-point quality gate

This is an internal studio rubric, not an external award formula.

A flagship public experience should target **90+ / 100** before Valtum considers it top-tier.

| Dimension | Weight |
|---|---:|
| Product-native concept / ownability | 15 |
| Composition / art direction | 15 |
| Media / visual evidence | 10 |
| Typography / editorial system | 8 |
| Interaction / motion meaning | 10 |
| Usability / task clarity | 10 |
| Mobile authorship | 10 |
| Accessibility / input resilience | 6 |
| Performance / stability | 6 |
| Engineering quality / maintainability | 5 |
| Content / proof / trust | 5 |
| **Total** | **100** |

## 6.1 Score interpretation

**0–2/10 equivalent**  
Unacceptable / template / AI-slop / obvious design failure.

**3–4/10**  
Functional but generic commercial design.

**5–6/10**  
Strong conventional professional work.

**7–8/10**  
Award-credible, distinctive, mature.

**9–10/10**  
Top-tier authored work where concept, craft, product truth, interaction, mobile and engineering reinforce each other.

The Personality Assessor rejection cycle proved why ordinary “clean and professional” scores must not be inflated.

---

# 7. The permanent anti-AI / anti-template constitution

The following rules are permanent unless the user explicitly overrides one for a specific project.

## 7.1 No generic AI aesthetic

Reject:

- purple/blue/cyan gradients;
- synthetic glow;
- neural mesh;
- floating brain;
- glowing sphere;
- glassy orb;
- particle face;
- random node network;
- “AI-powered” pill;
- fake chat bubbles as hero decoration;
- black background + neon grid.

AI is a capability, not a visual genre.

## 7.2 No gradient-based sophistication

No gradients for:

- backgrounds;
- text;
- buttons;
- borders;
- cards;
- glows;
- overlays.

If image readability requires an image-local shadow/tonal mask, it must be justified and restrained rather than used as brand styling.

## 7.3 No beige/cream agency cliché

Avoid default:

- ivory;
- cream;
- beige;
- warm luxury off-white.

A product can use a warm material palette if its real brand/art direction requires it, but Valtum must not default there because “design studios use cream.”

## 7.4 No split-color hero words

Do not color one hero keyword to create fake visual interest.

Hierarchy must come from:

- scale;
- position;
- weight;
- media;
- negative space;
- movement.

## 7.5 No generic left-copy/right-image hero

This remains one of the most important bans.

If the hero can be described as:

> heading on left, image/mockup on right, two buttons underneath

it needs a product-specific reason or it fails.

## 7.6 Header belongs to hero/opening

No detached floating pill header.

No generic white strip.

The header participates in the first composition.

## 7.7 No eyebrow system

Do not automatically place:

`01 / FEATURE`
`OUR APPROACH`
`AI INTELLIGENCE`
`03 — METHODOLOGY`

above every heading.

Small metadata is allowed when it is actual metadata.

Decorative pseudo-editorial labeling is rejected.

# 8. The most hated pattern — cards and TEXT–CONTAINER–CARD LOOP

This section is intentionally explicit because this failure has repeated across multiple generated designs.

## 8.1 Main marketing websites must not be built from card loops

Especially rejected:

- four horizontal cards;
- four vertical cards;
- 3×2 feature cards;
- icon + heading + paragraph cards;
- numbered process cards;
- trust cards;
- service cards;
- “why us” cards;
- framework cards;
- metric cards;
- bento for the sake of bento.

### Example failure

```text
Large heading
paragraph

[ card ][ card ][ card ][ card ]

Large heading
paragraph

[ card ][ card ][ card ]

Dark section

[ card ][ card ][ card ]
```

This is the anti-design pattern.

## 8.2 What to do instead

Represent the actual content as:

- image field;
- editorial list;
- interactive list;
- timeline;
- spatial sequence;
- diagram;
- large visual actor;
- comparison;
- map;
- scene;
- archive;
- image card;
- project chapter;
- product UI;
- media collage;
- continuous narrative;
- direct manipulation.

## 8.3 Image cards are explicitly allowed

The user has clearly approved **image-led cards**.

A good image card is:

- 80–100% media;
- text over image or in a small attached layer;
- carefully cropped;
- part of composition;
- interactive where useful.

Example:

**Career Worlds**  
Open career names on black → hover causes a large image card to appear/tilt/follow slightly → one concise phrase over image.

That is not the same thing as a text card.

## 8.4 The four-item rule

If a brief contains exactly four concepts, do **not** automatically make four equal cards.

Ask:

- Are they steps?
- dimensions?
- roles?
- evidence?
- states?
- priorities?
- filters?
- comparisons?

The representation should follow that answer.

---

# 9. Composition before components

A top-tier designer thinks in frames and relationships before component names.

## 9.1 Static frame gate

Before implementation, major pages need static keyframes.

At minimum:

- opening;
- transition;
- core product reveal;
- interactive state;
- closing;
- mobile opening;
- mobile core state.

If these still frames are not strong, motion is forbidden as a rescue mechanism.

## 9.2 Blur/silhouette gate

Blur the screenshot mentally.

Can you still distinguish:

- hero;
- product world;
- proof;
- dark chapter;
- interaction;
- final state?

If the page becomes repeated rectangles, fail.

## 9.3 Paragraph-hide gate

Hide long copy.

Does the visitor still understand:

- what this product is;
- what it does;
- what changes;
- what action exists?

If not, the design is relying on writing instead of representation.

## 9.4 Swap-logo test

Replace the brand name with a random SaaS logo.

If the design still fits perfectly, ownability is weak.

---

# 10. Valtum flagship website — current top-level constitution

The studio website must itself be a portfolio proof.

It should communicate:

> **Valtum can design and build difficult software beautifully.**

## 10.1 The protagonist

**The work.**

More specifically:

> the transformation from complex requirement to functioning product.

Not:

- office;
- team photo;
- laptop;
- AI orb;
- developer stock;
- abstract 3D thing.

## 10.2 Hero/opening direction

Do not pre-lock one layout globally, but the strongest standing direction remains:

- header integrated in the same visual field;
- large authored typography;
- real project artifacts entering the composition;
- product media at different depths/scales;
- no copy column;
- immediate proof that the studio makes real software.

The visitor should see project substance before reading a long manifesto.

## 10.3 Selected work

The five portfolio projects should **not** become five equal cards.

Better:

- each project becomes a chapter;
- different media geometry per project;
- product-specific background/visual system;
- concise role/scope/outcome;
- transition carries media into case study where useful.

## 10.4 Capability

Do not create:

`Web Development / AI / Mobile / Data / Design / Blockchain`

as six identical cards.

Capability should be expressed through:

- project evidence;
- a compact capability index;
- technical stack/context inside case studies;
- selected R&D;
- a capability field tied to work.

The site may communicate the studio's broader service range—websites/web apps, booking/marketplace systems, dashboards/backends, data/analytics, AI/automation, computer vision, Python/OpenCV, agents, Flutter mobile, and restrained Web3—without turning the homepage into a service catalog.

## 10.5 Case studies

Every flagship case study should document:

### Context
What organization/product/problem exists?

### Stakes
Why does it matter?

### Product truth
What actually works?

### Design thesis
What conceptual decision organizes the experience?

### UX
What difficult user journey was solved?

### Visual system
What belongs specifically to this product?

### Motion
What behavior communicates meaning?

### Mobile
How was the experience recomposed?

### Engineering
Architecture, performance, data, integration, deployment, relevant technical decisions.

### Evidence
Real UI, real screenshots, real flows, real supported outcomes.

### Reflection
Tradeoffs and learning.

### Credits
What Valtum actually did.

## 10.6 Studio commercial clarity

The site still needs:

- clear contact;
- what Valtum does;
- project suitability;
- global availability;
- process confidence;
- legal/business identity;
- proof.

Do not let the creative experience make a prospective client hunt for basic information.

---

# 11. Software-studio delivery model

The design brain must guide the business toward a high-end delivery experience.

## 11.1 Stage 0 — qualification

Understand:

- client;
- problem;
- budget range where appropriate;
- timeline;
- existing product;
- decision-makers;
- success metric;
- technical constraints;
- content/assets;
- legal/compliance.

## 11.2 Stage 1 — product archaeology

Audit:

- current product;
- backend;
- routes;
- states;
- data;
- content;
- brand;
- analytics;
- accessibility;
- performance;
- technical debt.

## 11.3 Stage 2 — design intelligence

Research:

- product domain;
- user expectations;
- competitors;
- adjacent best-in-class work;
- award references;
- interaction patterns;
- mobile app patterns;
- visual precedents.

## 11.4 Stage 3 — creative territories

Generate several genuinely different worlds.

A territory contains:

- truth;
- concept;
- protagonist;
- composition;
- media;
- motion;
- mobile;
- implementation implications;
- risk.

## 11.5 Stage 4 — concept lock + resource approval

The user/client approves:

- concept;
- fonts;
- color;
- imagery.

## 11.6 Stage 5 — static design

Design keyframes before motion.

## 11.7 Stage 6 — motion/interaction system

Define:

- state;
- trigger;
- transition;
- reversal;
- reduced motion;
- mobile equivalent.

## 11.8 Stage 7 — implementation contract

Coding agent receives exact instructions.

## 11.9 Stage 8 — source audit

Verify implementation truth.

## 11.10 Stage 9 — browser forensic review

Actual rendered design is judged.

## 11.11 Stage 10 — release + measurement

Measure:

- performance;
- conversion;
- usability;
- errors;
- analytics;
- feedback.

Iterate.

---

# 12. Engineering constitution derived from top studios

## 12.1 No universal framework religion

The right stack depends on the product.

Potential patterns:

- React/Next.js for complex interactive/product interfaces when appropriate;
- static/SSR/SSG where content/performance requires;
- headless commerce for complex commerce ecosystems;
- custom backend/API integration where product logic exists;
- Webflow for appropriate brand/CMS marketing surfaces when ownership and speed justify it;
- native/mobile frameworks for app-specific needs;
- WebGL only when the visual concept requires real-time rendering.

## 12.2 Semantic HTML first

Use native semantics before ARIA emulation.

- `button` for actions;
- `a` for navigation;
- form inputs with labels;
- headings in logical order;
- dialog/details where appropriate.

## 12.3 Design system ≠ visible component template

Use:

- tokens;
- primitives;
- spacing;
- typography roles;
- semantic states;
- accessibility patterns;
- motion tokens;
- image utilities.

Do not force visible macro-composition into a design-system card library.

## 12.4 Motion architecture

One clear conductor per page-level sequence.

Avoid scattered independent timelines that fight.

Use:

- GSAP for complex reversible scroll choreography;
- CSS/WAAPI for simple state;
- Framer Motion for product/app layout presence where useful;
- WebGL/Three.js only for genuine spatial requirements;
- native View Transitions as progressive enhancement where appropriate.

## 12.5 Progressive enhancement

If custom rendering fails:

- content remains;
- navigation remains;
- action remains;
- essential product understanding remains.

The K95/Igloo/Oryzo/Aether forensic failures remain permanent warnings.

## 12.6 CMS/editor ownership

Choose CMS architecture based on:

- content frequency;
- editors;
- locales;
- commerce;
- asset system;
- preview;
- structured content;
- deployment model.

Do not choose CMS for developer fashion.

## 12.7 Testing

At flagship level:

- unit/component tests;
- integration tests;
- accessibility checks;
- responsive browser review;
- key interaction review;
- performance profiling;
- visual regression where useful.

But automated tests do not approve art direction.

---

# 13. Performance quality gate

Current web quality targets remain:

- **LCP ≤ 2.5 s**
- **INP ≤ 200 ms**
- **CLS ≤ 0.1**

at the 75th percentile where field measurement is available.

## 13.1 Creative-site rule

Performance budget is part of the concept.

If the concept requires:

- 4K video;
- 3D;
- many photos;
- canvas;
- filters;

design the fallback, preload strategy and mobile substitution at concept stage.

## 13.2 Media

- hero LCP candidate eager;
- correct dimensions;
- `srcset`;
- `sizes`;
- AVIF/WebP where appropriate;
- art-directed mobile crop;
- below-fold lazy;
- do not preload entire gallery.

## 13.3 Avoid performance theater

A branded loader does not solve slow performance.

It is allowed only when essential.

---

# 14. Mobile — design it like an app, not a compressed site

This remains one of the user's strongest requirements.

## 14.1 Independent composition

Desktop DOM may be reusable where semantically helpful, but mobile composition must be designed separately.

Ask:

- What is the mobile first viewport?
- What becomes the main actor?
- Which media disappears?
- What crop changes?
- What becomes tap?
- What becomes swipe?
- What becomes bottom-fixed?
- What content is deferred?
- What order changes?

## 14.2 Mobile marketing

A marketing page should feel native to the phone:

- fewer simultaneous actors;
- larger visual focus;
- short text;
- strong vertical rhythm;
- touch-safe interactive lists;
- no tiny desktop navigation;
- no accidental giant blank spaces.

## 14.3 Mobile product UI

Operational apps:

- task first;
- state obvious;
- next action obvious;
- errors recoverable;
- no unnecessary motion;
- system status legible.

---

# 15. Accessibility — premium means everyone can use it

Follow WCAG 2.2 as the baseline.

Key standing rules:

- logical keyboard order;
- visible focus;
- no focus obscured by sticky chrome;
- target size minimum respected;
- prefer ~44×44 for important touch actions;
- drag has an alternative where dragging is not essential;
- reduced motion is an alternate composition;
- color is not the only meaning;
- essential information is not canvas-only.

Accessibility must be tested by the whole implementation workflow, not delegated only to final QA.

---

# 16. Media art direction — studio-grade standard

## 16.1 Major asset gate

The user has final approval over:

- primary imagery;
- typography;
- palette.

No coding agent silently locks them.

## 16.2 Stock photography

Stock is allowed only when it looks like deliberate art direction.

Reject:

- corporate handshake;
- generic developer;
- laptop at 45°;
- smiling team pointing at screen;
- artificial “AI professional”;
- inconsistent lighting.

## 16.3 Generated imagery

Generated imagery can be used when deliberately art-directed and approved.

It must not look:

- synthetic;
- uncanny;
- glossy AI stock;
- inconsistent in hands/faces/materials;
- stylistically disconnected.

## 16.4 Product screenshots

Real product UI is often the strongest media.

Treat screenshots as:

- evidence;
- typography;
- object;
- texture;
- sequence.

Do not always place them in browser/laptop mockups.

---

# 17. Typography — no “premium font” shortcut

The research corpus contains many type systems.

There is no ecosystem-wide final family.

The studio chooses based on product.

## 17.1 What typography must do

- communicate;
- establish hierarchy;
- create geometry;
- carry brand voice;
- support data;
- remain readable;
- perform on mobile.

## 17.2 Valtum flagship

The Valtum site can use an authored grotesk/display system, but should not default to:

- Inter clone look;
- ultra-bold startup type;
- fake luxury serif.

The final family must be reviewed in keyframes.

## 17.3 Product-specific differentiation

- KT: operational legibility + numerals.
- Dubai: editorial warmth + transaction clarity.
- Math: authoritative math + interface legibility.
- Personality: human but analytical.
- Aegis: precise operational reading.

---

# 18. Color — product native, never trendy by default

No single palette is applied to all six.

## 18.1 Valtum

Let project media bring color.

The studio shell can remain strong and authored without turning every project into “Valtum green.”

Earlier green experiments are historical, not binding.

## 18.2 Personality Assessor

Do not auto-copy orange from the current visual reference.

## 18.3 KT

Status colors must mean status.

## 18.4 Dubai

Photography can carry chroma.

## 18.5 Math

Learning/data color must be semantic.

## 18.6 Aegis

Alert/status colors must be operational, not neon atmosphere.

---

# 19. Motion system — meaning before spectacle

A reusable Valtum motion vocabulary:

### Reveal
Information becomes available.

### Carry
An actor survives into the next state.

### Exchange
One representation becomes another.

### Resolve
Complexity settles.

### Reorder
Same elements change priority.

### Inspect
User asks for deeper evidence.

### Compare
Two states are made visually relational.

### Route
Selected object carries into a new route.

### Return
Later evidence/progress changes an earlier profile/state.

### Propagate
One action creates consequences across multiple dimensions.

The motion vocabulary should appear differently per product.

---

# 20. Five portfolio product constitutions — refreshed

## 20.1 KT Courier

**North star:** movement made accountable.

### Product-native visual material
- route;
- order;
- delivery state;
- driver/store/customer roles;
- timestamps;
- proof;
- exceptions;
- settlement/payment where real.

### Avoid
- courier holding box hero;
- map as decoration;
- generic logistics cards;
- fake live delivery;
- fake tracking.

### Marketing
Show one delivery moving through the system.

Task-first.

---

## 20.2 Dubai Booking Marketplace

**North star:** desire becomes a trustworthy transaction.

### Hero
Real experience/place photography.

### Story
discover → compare → trust → availability → book.

### Avoid
- gold/black luxury cliché;
- generic skyline;
- excessive smooth scroll around booking controls;
- hidden price/availability.

---

## 20.3 Math Intellect

**North star:** understanding becomes manipulable.

### Protagonist
Mathematical relationship.

### Hero
Interactive idea, not stock.

### Product
Model/assumption/result/uncertainty.

### Avoid
- AI orb;
- generic dashboard cards;
- rainbow intelligence theater;
- fake simulation.

---

## 20.4 Personality Assessor

**North star:** professional complexity becomes interpretable without becoming a label.

### Current latest reference-locked visual family

Hero:
- centered bold modern sans;
- white canvas;
- multi-image professional masonry;
- integrated CTA;
- header in same opening.

Whole site:
- image-dominant;
- varied silhouettes;
- light/dark rhythm;
- image-first cards;
- product overlays;
- black interactive Career Worlds list;
- designed footer.

### Permanent lessons from failure
- no text/card loop;
- no giant serif-as-premium;
- no fake evidence lines;
- no giant trust cards;
- no fake testimonial;
- no preselected demo answer;
- no unsupported privacy claims;
- no global overflow concealment.

---

## 20.5 Aegis Senital

**North star:** evidence → context → action.

### Protagonist
One event becoming understandable.

### Avoid
- military/tactical copy;
- cyberpunk;
- neon detection boxes as decoration;
- fake confidence;
- “AI security” imagery.

### Mobile
What happened? Where? Evidence? State? Action?

# 21. Valtum case-study standard — evidence-rich, not award-gallery-only

Each case study should have three reading depths.

## Fast scan

- problem;
- product;
- role;
- key visual;

## Medium scan

- design thesis;
- user journey;
- system;
- interface;
- mobile;

## Deep read

- constraints;

The page should allow a client to evaluate:

- taste;

# 22. Content voice for Valtum Studio

The tone:

- intelligent;
- exact;
- confident;
- technically literate;
- human;
- concise.

Not:

- inflated;
- buzzword-heavy;
- AI-written;
- childish;
- luxury-agency vague.

## Avoid

- “elevate”
- “unlock”
- “redefine the future”
- “cutting-edge”
- “seamless”
- “game-changing”
- “transformative solutions”
- “we craft digital experiences that inspire”

unless a specific evidence-backed sentence genuinely requires the term.

## Prefer

Specific verbs:

- design;
- build;
- ship;
- integrate;
- automate;
- model;
- verify;
- scale;
- measure;
- simplify;
- redesign;
- launch.

# 23. Conversion without destroying art direction

A top-tier studio site is a business tool.

A prospective client should be able to answer quickly:

- What does Valtum build?
- Is this studio capable of my problem?
- What proof exists?
- What is the quality bar?
- How do I start?
- Is the studio credible globally?

The contact path should be unmistakable.

Do not make users complete an artistic scavenger hunt to send a project inquiry.

---

# 24. How coding agents receive work

A Codex contract should include:

1. Authority order.
2. Source truth.
3. Scope.
4. Preserve/delete boundaries.
5. Exact current visual references.
6. Protagonist.
7. Page/state architecture.
8. Geometry.
9. Copy.
10. Asset manifest.
11. Typography.
12. Color.
13. Motion.
14. Responsive/mobile.
15. Accessibility.
16. Performance.
17. Product-truth guardrails.
18. Tests.
19. Browser screenshots/states.
20. Completion report.

The agent does not get:

> “Make it premium.”

It gets:

> exact implementation behavior.

---

# 25. Post-Codex source audit

Never trust the completion report automatically.

Inspect the source for:

- old visual system still present;
- default answers;
- fake data;
- fake people;
- fake trust;
- unsupported claims;
- copied colors;
- rejected assets;
- global overflow hiding;
- motion accessibility;
- duplicated page shells;
- mobile compromises.

The Personality Assessor correction cycle is now a canonical training example.

---

# 26. Browser acceptance — the final authority

After source truth passes, inspect real rendered states.

## Desktop
At least:
- 1440×900;
- 1366×768.

## Tablet
- 1024×768;
- 768×1024.

## Mobile
- 430×932;
- 390×844;
- 375×812;
- 360×800;
- 320 where relevant.

## Inspect:
- opening;
- first transition;
- strongest visual scene;
- active interaction;
- dark/light transition;
- footer;
- secondary route;
- product task;
- mobile interaction.

Do not accept from one full-page screenshot.

---

# 27. 9+ visual forensic checklist

Before saying “approved,” ask:

## Concept
Could this visual idea belong only to this product/studio?

## Composition
Does every scene have a strong silhouette?

## Media
Are images proof/geometry/world?

## Type
Does typography do more than become large?

## Cards
Has text-card thinking returned?

## Rhythm
Do sections vary pressure?

## Motion
Does it explain state/continuity?

## Mobile
Is it authored independently?

## Product truth
Is every claim real?

## Accessibility
Can users operate it beyond pointer?

## Performance
Does the intended world actually load?

## Ending
Does the site resolve?

If any flagship dimension remains ~5/10, the site is not 9+ overall.

The fresh studio research should influence **how Valtum thinks**, never how it looks by default.

Do not create:

Surface treatment remains Valtum's.

# 29. The Valtum “designer brain” in one sequence

When receiving a new brief:

### Step 1
What is true?

### Step 2
What is hard to understand?

### Step 3
What should the person remember?

### Step 4
What visual material already exists inside the product?

### Step 5
What could persist for 20–40 seconds without becoming decoration?

### Step 6
What should the visitor manipulate?

### Step 7
What proof belongs early?

### Step 8
What can be deleted?

### Step 9
What does mobile become?

### Step 10
What technology is actually required?

### Step 11
Can the still frame win before motion?

### Step 12
Can it survive accessibility/performance constraints?

### Step 13
Can a coding agent implement it without inventing design?

### Step 14
Does the browser actually look as good as the spec?

# 31. Research conclusions added in this final version

The new research materially strengthens the previous brain in twelve ways.

1. **Valtum must position as a product/software studio, not a web agency.**
2. **Senior involvement is a premium differentiator.**
3. **Brand, product and engineering should reinforce one another.**
4. **No single framework/stack defines the studio.**
5. **High-end case studies need technical and business evidence.**
6. **Accessibility is a team design practice, not compliance at the end.**
7. **Creative technology must respect technical constraints/performance.**
8. **Australian origin can coexist with a global design standard.**
9. **Image/media art direction is a strategic capability, not decoration.**
10. **Award criteria reward overall experience, not visual spectacle alone.**
11. **Component systems should disappear underneath authored composition.**
12. **The studio's five portfolio products are strongest when their differences are made visible, not normalized.**

## Unified Master Constitution, Research Archive, Rejection Ledger, Product-Specific Design Doctrine & Creative Frontend Engineering System

# 0. Why this file exists

This is not a moodboard, a style guide, a collection of trendy rules, or a single-project specification.

It is the consolidated operating brain for the studio's UI/UX, visual design, product design, content design, motion design, responsive design, accessibility, performance, and creative frontend engineering work. It merges the complete surviving 46-file research/specification corpus, the project's accumulated rejection learning, the latest Personality Assessor reset and reference-locked direction, Math Intellect's C54/C55 negative controls and product constitution, KT Courier's product/engineering handoff context, the live forensic studies, the user's Pinterest/reference-board evidence, and the newest research refresh completed on 18 August 2026.

The purpose is not to force every product into one visible style.

The purpose is to create one **quality system and decision system** that can generate very different, product-native interfaces without falling back into template habits.

The studio portfolio currently includes:

- Volterm/Valtum Studio — flagship studio and portfolio.
- Personality Assessor.
- KT Courier.
- Dubai Booking Marketplace.
- Math Intellect.
- Aegis Senital.

The common DNA is **craft, authorship, product truth, clarity, visual intelligence, motion with meaning, mobile intentionality, accessibility, performance, and implementation exactness**.

The common DNA is **not** a shared palette, shared hero, shared card system, shared WebGL treatment, shared typography costume, shared gradient, shared navigation shell, or shared motion effect.

---

# 1. Authority order

When instructions conflict, use this authority order unless the user explicitly overrides it in the current conversation:

1. **The user's latest explicit instruction.**
2. **Verified product truth in the current repository/backend/business requirements.**
3. **This 18 August 2026 unified master constitution.**
4. **The current product-specific approved visual direction.**
5. **Current rendered-browser evidence.**
6. **Current primary/official research evidence.**
7. **Earlier project-specific specifications and experiments.**
8. **Historical explorations preserved in the source archive.**
9. **General web-design convention.**

A beautiful idea cannot override product truth.

A passing test suite cannot override a visually failed browser.

A previous concept cannot override a later user rejection.

A famous reference cannot override product-specific semantics.

A coding agent cannot promote its own interpretation above the design authority.

---

# 2. Role model — who decides what

## 2.1 Chief design/architecture authority

ChatGPT acts as:

- chief UI/UX architect;
- senior product designer;
- senior visual designer;
- creative director;
- interaction and motion architect;
- content-structure designer;
- senior frontend design engineer;
- responsive/mobile design authority;
- accessibility/performance design reviewer;
- research synthesizer;
- source-truth auditor;
- browser visual QA authority.

Its responsibility is not merely to suggest attractive surfaces. It must determine:

- what the product actually does;
- what the visitor/user must understand;
- what visual protagonist belongs to that truth;
- what interaction model belongs to the task;
- what should persist;
- what should move;
- what should remain quiet;
- what the mobile experience should become;
- what content should be removed;
- what copy is defensible;
- what media is needed;
- what implementation technology is justified;
- what a coding agent must do exactly;
- whether the rendered browser truly passes.

## 2.2 Coding-agent role

Codex or another coding model is an **implementation agent**, not an autonomous art director.

A coding agent must not:

- reinterpret the design concept;
- invent missing product claims;
- choose a new visual style because implementation is easier;
- substitute generic stock;
- redesign a route because the contract is hard;
- turn a visual concept into a component-library pattern;
- introduce a new animation framework merely because it knows it;
- create fake metrics, testimonials, trust claims, scores or scientific authority;
- silently weaken mobile;
- declare visual success from tests/build output;
- alter Git history unless explicitly authorized.

The agent should receive, where relevant:

- exact route scope;
- exact content;
- exact approved media;
- asset provenance;
- responsive crops;
- geometry;
- typography roles;
- palette;
- section/state silhouettes;
- interaction states;
- motion ownership;
- accessibility behavior;
- reduced-motion behavior;
- failure/empty/loading behavior;
- performance budgets;
- cleanup boundaries;
- validation commands;
- browser acceptance screenshots/states.

---

# 3. The master operating equation

The studio's design process is:

**evidence → diagnosis → product-specific hypothesis → creative territories → protagonist → visual world → static composition → interaction → mobile composition → accessibility/performance → exact implementation contract → source audit → rendered-browser forensic review**

Do not reverse this sequence.

Specifically, do not begin with:

- "hero";
- "three feature cards";
- "dark section";
- "bento";
- "dashboard cards";
- "GSAP animation";
- "3D object";
- "premium font";
- "modern gradient";
- "AI visual";
- "left copy / right image";
- "what can we reuse from the previous site?"

Those are implementation or surface questions. They are downstream.

The upstream questions are:

1. What is true?
2. What is difficult to understand?
3. What should the visitor remember?
4. What is the product's own visual material?
5. What can become the persistent protagonist?
6. What changes state?
7. What should the user directly manipulate?
8. What proof should arrive?
9. What remains unresolved?
10. What should the next action be?

---

# 4. Strict top-tier quality judge

The benchmark is not "professional enough for a normal SaaS client."

The benchmark is top-tier authored digital work: Awwwards-level creative direction, strong studio case-study quality, and the standard of interfaces that can credibly represent a high-end studio.

The scoring model must therefore be strict.

A clean conventional SaaS landing page with good typography, spacing and development may still be only **1–3/10** against this target if:

- its structure is generic;
- it could belong to another product;
- the composition is mostly copy plus cards;
- photography merely decorates;
- mobile is stacked desktop;
- motion is reveal theater;
- the page has no memorable protagonist;
- each route shares the same silhouette;
- the footer is boilerplate;
- the hero is a banner rather than a world.

A site moves toward **9+/10** only when:

- visual authorship is obvious in still screenshots;
- the concept belongs to the product;
- media, type, spacing and interaction operate as one system;
- the blur/silhouette remains distinctive;
- visual states survive without paragraphs;
- the mobile version feels intentionally authored;
- the site explains or demonstrates something through design rather than copy alone;
- interactions have semantic consequence;
- transitions preserve identity where appropriate;
- route variation exists within a coherent identity;
- accessibility and performance are engineered rather than bolted on;
- the browser has been forensically reviewed at real viewports.

## 4.1 Award-weight mindset

Current Awwwards public score pages continue to expose the familiar weighting:

- Design — 40%
- Usability — 30%
- Creativity — 20%
- Content — 10%

This does not mean "design for a jury." It means the user's repeated intuition was correct: a site with accurate content but generic design, generic usability patterns and little creative authorship cannot reach the intended tier.

Development recognition also cares about clean code, semantics, technologies, accessibility, SEO, performance, animation and responsive design. Creative direction and engineering quality are therefore inseparable at this level.

---

# 5. The anti-template constitution

## 5.1 The canonical failure: TEXT–CONTAINER–CARD LOOP

The most important negative control across the entire corpus is the **TEXT–CONTAINER–CARD LOOP**:

> heading → paragraph → rounded container → cards/rows → another heading → another container → another card system

Changing:

- border radius;
- shadow;
- background;
- heading font;
- card orientation;
- line color;
- icon shape

does not fix this.

It is still container-first design.

The rule is:

> **representation first, container second.**

Ask what the information should become before asking what box should contain it.

## 5.2 Cards are not banned; card thinking is

Cards are legitimate when the information anatomy earns independent containment.

Examples:

- a saved assessment;
- a booking item;
- a delivery;
- a report;
- a product;
- a standalone alert;
- a transaction;
- an image-first editorial item;
- a discrete dashboard module with independent action/state.

Cards are rejected when they exist because the designer needs a default answer for layout.

### Image-first card exception

A major later user clarification is binding:

**Image cards are acceptable and often desirable when the image is the visual surface.**

A good image card:

- is primarily media;
- uses intentional crop and subject direction;
- may carry concise text over the media;
- can reveal more media on hover/tap;
- participates in a larger composition;
- has a distinct semantic reason to exist.

A rejected text card:

- icon;
- title;
- paragraph;
- border;
- repeated 3–8 times;
- little or no visual/proof material.

A useful heuristic:

> If removing the image leaves the "card" essentially intact, it is probably the wrong kind of card for a flagship marketing experience.

## 5.3 Bento

Bento is not a standing style.

It is allowed only when the information anatomy and product identity genuinely require semantically differentiated modules.

It must not become:

- generic feature bento;
- "AI dashboard" bento;
- agency-service bento;
- automatic answer to a sparse page.

## 5.4 Macro containers

Reject:

- giant white rounded rectangles enclosing an entire chapter;
- repeated 28px-radius chapter modules as the primary page grammar;
- giant light-gray sheets that make every section look like a dashboard widget.

A reference may use rounded modules effectively. Transfer the **rhythm and image dominance**, not the universal container surface.

At least some major chapters should bleed, overlap, merge with media, or have no visible enclosing rectangle.

---

# 6. Hard never-to-do list

Unless the user explicitly overrides a specific item for a specific project, do not use:

- generic AI-template aesthetics;
- gradients as a design language;
- blue/purple/cyan "AI" gradients;
- generic glows;
- glassmorphism as default identity;
- beige/cream/ivory/warm-off-white agency cliché;
- fake luxury black/gold language;
- generic cyberpunk;
- generic dark "cinematic" stock;
- random 3D orb;
- particle brain;
- glowing human silhouette;
- floating AI sphere;
- hero keyword with another color/gradient;
- generic left-text/right-image hero;
- detached floating pill navbar;
- header in a separate visual strip above the hero;
- decorative horizontal divider rules;
- tiny label + line pseudo-editorial system;
- eyebrow/kicker text as a routine system;
- visible editorial numbering as a routine system;
- "01 / 02 / 03" labels added for style;
- universal extra-bold sans as the definition of premium;
- universal giant serif as the definition of premium;
- generic fade-up motion across every element;
- bouncy microinteraction soup;
- selected-card hover lift applied everywhere;
- page-wide parallax merely for spectacle;
- scroll snapping as a default;
- long pinned sections that hide content;
- IntersectionObserver swaps masquerading as authored motion;
- global `overflow-x: hidden` used to conceal layout defects;
- internal scrollbars inside marketing scenes;
- fake loading percentages;
- artificial minimum loader durations;
- fake "Live" badges;
- fake social proof;
- fake user counts;
- fake testimonials;
- fake reviews;
- fake community numbers;
- fake ROI calculators;
- fake confidence percentages;
- fake charts;
- fake activity streams;
- fake security claims;
- fake encryption claims;
- fake science claims;
- fake certifications;
- fake "validated" language without evidence;
- unsupported privacy promises;
- unsupported retention promises;
- generic privacy grids styled as trust theater;
- fake AI-generated "insight" appearing selected on first load;
- preselected illustrative answers when the user has not acted;
- missing-data visualization as invented midpoint/zero;
- desktop cards simply stacked vertically on mobile;
- hover-only essential interaction without touch/keyboard equivalent;
- custom drag with no non-drag alternative when the interaction is not inherently spatial;
- smooth scrolling on operational/auth/product-task surfaces merely for visual taste.

---

# 7. Product truth outranks visual ambition

Every product-specific site begins with a source audit.

The design system may not invent:

- features;
- APIs;
- analytics;
- progress;
- data freshness;
- confidence;
- scientific validation;
- privacy policy;
- deletion timing;
- retention timing;
- geography;
- pricing;
- inventory;
- testimonials;
- company scale;
- integrations.

Use evidence labels internally:

- VERIFIED PRODUCT TRUTH
- DIRECTLY OBSERVED
- TECHNICALLY VERIFIED
- DOCUMENTED
- INFERRED
- DESIGN LOCK
- ILLUSTRATIVE EXAMPLE
- NOT VERIFIED

When a marketing visual uses illustrative data, disclose it locally and clearly.

Missing data is not:

- 0;
- 50%;
- average;
- midpoint;
- placeholder line;
- fabricated trend.

Missing data is:

- Not available;
- Not enough evidence;
- Not enough history;
- No completed assessment yet;
- no point plotted.

---

# 8. Composition doctrine

## 8.1 Design the silhouette before the details

Every major scene must pass the blur test.

If text becomes gray blocks, the composition should still reveal:

- focal point;
- scale;
- balance/imbalance;
- media geometry;
- pressure;
- negative space;
- state hierarchy;
- chapter difference.

If every scene becomes:

> heading blob + paragraph blob + rectangle blob

the art direction is not finished.

## 8.2 Section pressure

A long page should vary pressure.

Use combinations of:

- compression;
- release;
- full bleed;
- close crop;
- wide environmental image;
- sparse white field;
- dark high-pressure state;
- large media;
- small proof;
- interactive field;
- editorial list;
- direct task state.

Do not make every section equally spacious and equally centered.

## 8.3 Asymmetry

Asymmetry is useful when it creates:

- attention;
- direction;
- narrative tension;
- media hierarchy;
- edge tension.

It is not useful when it is random displacement.

## 8.4 Negative space

Whitespace is a structural material.

Do not fill empty space with:

- extra cards;
- explanatory copy;
- decorative numbers;
- labels;
- lines;
- badges.

The stronger the protagonist, the more surrounding UI can become quiet.

## 8.5 Type/media interlock

Typography may:

- sit behind media;
- cross a crop;
- become a spatial plane;
- frame imagery;
- create intentional holes for media;
- be partially occluded when legibility is still protected.

This should not become a repeated trick.

The relationship must emerge from the subject geometry.

---

# 9. Header and navigation doctrine

## 9.1 The header belongs to the opening world

The opening header is not a separate rectangle.

It should share:

- canvas;
- grid;
- contrast logic;
- spatial system;
- visual atmosphere

with the hero/opening scene.

No automatic border-bottom.

No detached white strip unless the product/task explicitly requires a conventional app shell.

## 9.2 Header transitions

A header may change after the opening world exits:

- dark → light;
- overlay → compact sticky;
- expanded → reduced;
- visual navigation → utility navigation.

The change should be caused by the scene state, not by a generic "after 100px add blur" rule.

## 9.3 Menus

A large visual site may use a full-screen menu as an authored intermission.

But:

- focus must be managed;
- Escape must work;
- background scroll must lock where appropriate;
- focus returns to the trigger;
- mobile targets must be generous;
- route changes close the menu;
- essential navigation must remain discoverable.

---

# 10. Footer doctrine

The footer is the final state of the story.

It must still contain practical utility:

- navigation;
- contact;
- legal;
- social;
- copyright;
- relevant business information.

But it should feel prepared by the preceding scene.

Strong footer patterns observed in research:

- persistent protagonist returns;
- large wordmark becomes final visual landscape;
- final CTA resolves the page's central question;
- product/brand object becomes totem;
- final media and utility coexist.

Reject:

- generic 4-column directory appended after the design ends;
- giant centered CTA that has no relationship to the preceding narrative;
- a footer visually imported from a component library.

---

# 11. Typography doctrine

Typography is not simply a scale table.

It has four roles:

1. **Reading typography** — long-form comprehension.
2. **Interface typography** — actions, states, navigation, labels, numerals.
3. **Editorial typography** — pacing, voice, contrast, chapter character.
4. **Spatial typography** — geometry and depth within composition.

## 11.1 Type selection

Do not lock a font because it feels "premium."

Select based on:

- brand character;
- product domain;
- legibility;
- numeral quality;
- language support;
- variable axes;
- available licensed files;
- performance;
- mathematical notation needs;
- dense dashboard needs;
- mobile behavior.

Prefer fewer families.

A highly customized site usually needs **one strong primary family** and, only where justified, one contrasting secondary role.

## 11.2 Historical typography directions

The archive contains several project-specific typography experiments:

- Source Serif + Source Sans;
- Instrument Sans + Newsreader;
- Inter Tight + Inter;
- Mona Sans;
- mathematical sans + STIX Two Math;
- other research candidates.

These are not globally locked.

Later user direction can supersede an earlier project font choice.

## 11.3 Personality Assessor current direction

For the latest reference-locked Personality Assessor direction, a modern bold grotesk/sans-led system is appropriate. The later reference-locked work moved away from the repetitive giant-serif system because the serif had become a generic "premium editorial" crutch.

The current implementation path used Inter Tight for display and Inter for UI/body as a practical production choice. Treat this as product-specific, not an ecosystem font mandate.

---

# 12. Color and material doctrine

## 12.1 No universal studio palette across all portfolio products

Each product derives color from:

- product semantics;
- approved brand;
- media art direction;
- state meaning;
- data meaning;
- accessibility.

The portfolio shares craft, not a paint bucket.

## 12.2 Standing bans

- no generic purple/blue AI;
- no default cream/beige studio surface;
- no gradient sophistication;
- no dark mode by prestige;
- no neon security language by default;
- no gold Dubai cliché;
- no rainbow charts for personality/math simply because many dimensions exist.

## 12.3 Accent

Accent should be sparse.

It may indicate:

- action;
- current state;
- selected evidence;
- active item;
- identity gesture;
- meaningful semantic state.

Do not pre-lock a reference site's accent simply because the reference is admired.

The Personality Assessor reference-locked iteration specifically taught this: the bright orange/coral from the Granger reference should not automatically become Personality Assessor's brand color.

## 12.4 Semantic color

Semantic state colors remain separate from brand accent:

- success;
- warning;
- error;
- informational;
- inactive;
- verified/selected if semantically appropriate.

Charts use controlled semantic assignment, not decoration.

---

# 13. Image and media doctrine

## 13.1 Media is geometry

Images should not be inserted after layout.

They influence:

- grid;
- crop;
- scale;
- subject direction;
- negative space;
- type placement;
- transition;
- scene pressure.

## 13.2 Every major image must do a job

A major image should:

- explain;
- prove;
- locate;
- demonstrate;
- establish world;
- create emotional proximity;
- provide product evidence;
- carry transition;
- establish rhythm.

"Looks cinematic" is not a sufficient job.

## 13.3 Coherent image ensembles

A hero with multiple photographs is judged as **one ensemble**.

Check:

- lighting;
- lens language;
- crop character;
- color grade;
- subject diversity;
- wardrobe;
- environment;
- resolution;
- background noise;
- commercial-stock feel;
- AI-generation artifacts.

Seven individually good photographs can still create a weak hero.

## 13.4 Responsive art direction

Do not rely on one `object-fit: cover` crop for every viewport.

For major media, specify:

- desktop source/crop;
- tablet crop;
- mobile source/crop;
- focal point;
- aspect ratio;
- object-position;
- whether an alternate source is required.

Use `<picture>`, `srcset`, `sizes`, responsive derivatives and intrinsic dimensions.

## 13.5 Image provenance

Maintain a manifest:

- internal ID;
- source;
- original URL/source ID;
- photographer/creator where applicable;
- license/provenance;
- original dimensions;
- role;
- desktop crop;
- mobile crop;
- alt text;
- derivative paths.

No reference screenshot crops should silently become production photography.

---

# 14. Motion doctrine

Motion is a semantic system.

Use a small vocabulary such as:

- Reveal
- Carry
- Exchange
- Propagate
- Accumulate
- Resolve
- Compare
- Inspect
- Route
- Reframe
- Reorder
- Focus
- Return

Each motion has:

- trigger;
- meaning;
- state A;
- transition;
- state B;
- reversal;
- interruption behavior;
- reduced-motion equivalent.

## 14.1 Keyframes first

Design still states before motion.

A weak still frame plus impressive animation is still a weak design.

For flagship scenes:

1. opening keyframe;
2. transition entry;
3. midpoint;
4. settled state;
5. reverse midpoint;
6. mobile equivalent;
7. reduced-motion equivalent.

If the still compositions do not reach the target, do not ask motion to rescue them.

## 14.2 Reversibility

Major scroll-linked state sequences must work:

- forward slowly;
- forward quickly;
- stop halfway;
- reverse slowly;
- reverse rapidly;
- small oscillating input;
- resize mid-state;
- route back.

A threshold-triggered one-shot animation is not enough for a semantic state journey.

## 14.3 Motion restraint

Use motion where it:

- explains state;
- preserves identity;
- shows causality;
- gives feedback;
- demonstrates product behavior;
- changes hierarchy;
- carries a selected object into a new context.

Do not animate because:

- there is scroll;
- the section entered viewport;
- an element can bounce;
- a library supports parallax.

---

# 15. Scroll doctrine

## 15.1 Native first

Native scroll is the baseline.

Smooth scroll is an art-direction tool, not a universal requirement.

## 15.2 Smooth-scroll eligibility

Consider smoothing only for appropriate storytelling routes when:

- desktop/laptop;
- sufficiently large viewport;
- fine pointer;
- reduced motion off;
- interaction remains responsive;
- native scrollbar semantics remain usable;
- there is a meaningful benefit.

Avoid or remove smoothing for:

- auth;
- assessment questions;
- checkout;
- forms;
- dashboards;
- security operations;
- dense analytics;
- touch mobile;
- reduced-motion users.

## 15.3 One scroll owner

Do not stack:

- Lenis;
- ScrollSmoother;
- custom virtual scroll;
- nested scroll hijackers

on the same page.

One clear conductor owns the experience.

## 15.4 Pin the stage; animate inside

If a narrative requires a persistent stage, pin/stick the stage and animate its internal actors.

Do not continuously transform the pinned element itself if it compromises measurements/behavior.

## 15.5 Horizontal movement requires semantic reason

Good reasons:

- progression;
- collection;
- spatial traversal;
- time;
- sequence.

Bad reason:

- "award sites have horizontal sections."

On mobile, most desktop scroll-driven horizontal sequences should become:

- vertical narrative;
- direct swipe;
- snap rail;
- one-state-per-screen/task;
- user-controlled gallery.

---

# 16. Technology ownership

Technology follows concept.

## 16.1 GSAP

Use when the experience needs:

- precise timelines;
- scroll-linked progress;
- reversible state sequences;
- shared visual continuity;
- complex coordinated DOM/SVG transforms;
- ScrollTrigger;
- Flip.

Use responsive setup/cleanup with current GSAP media-query/context patterns.

## 16.2 CSS / WAAPI / native browser

Use for:

- hover/focus;
- small state transitions;
- simple reveal;
- transform/opacity microfeedback;
- native scroll snapping;
- view transitions as progressive enhancement where appropriate.

## 16.3 Motion / Framer Motion

Useful inside product applications for:

- layout state;
- presence;
- protected-app transitions;
- component-level state changes.

Do not automatically use it for global route crossfades or marketing animation.

## 16.4 Anime.js

Historical specifications explored Anime.js v4 for local DOM/SVG motion.

It is a tool, not a standing identity.

Use only if the current product architecture benefits from it and it does not create redundant ownership with GSAP.

## 16.5 Rive

Use for authored vector/state-machine interaction where:

- the animation itself carries product meaning;
- the state machine is easier to maintain than hand-coded SVG/DOM;
- accessible fallback exists.

## 16.6 WebGL / Three.js

Use only when the concept truly needs:

- persistent 3D object;
- spatial world;
- shader/material behavior;
- data/world visualization that cannot be represented well in 2D;
- direct manipulation with genuine explanatory value.

Never use WebGL to manufacture prestige.

Progressive enhancement is mandatory.

The forensic reports repeatedly showed how all-or-nothing WebGL can turn a highly authored site into a blank/fallback experience.

---

# 17. Mobile = independent composition

The user's mobile requirement is stronger than "responsive."

The mobile experience should feel like it was designed for the phone as a primary product surface.

## 17.1 Mobile questions

For every desktop scene ask:

- What is the phone user's primary task?
- Which actor survives?
- Which actor disappears?
- What becomes full width?
- What becomes bottom-sheet or inline?
- What moves to the thumb zone?
- What replaces hover?
- Does horizontal become swipe or vertical?
- Does the hero need fewer images?
- Does type need different line breaks?
- Does the order change?
- Should the task become one screen at a time?

## 17.2 App-native principles

Strong mobile patterns include:

- one clear primary task per screen;
- controls near comfortable thumb reach;
- direct state feedback;
- safe-area awareness;
- minimal persistent chrome;
- 44×44-ish preferred touch controls for important actions;
- no tiny desktop sidebars;
- no tiny centered cards floating inside huge blank viewport;
- no dense multi-column charts;
- no essential hover;
- no accidental internal scrolling.

## 17.3 Reflow

Normal content should remain usable at narrow widths without two-dimensional scrolling.

Two-dimensional interaction is acceptable only where meaning truly requires it, such as:

- maps;
- diagrams;
- some mathematical surfaces;
- wide data tables;
- specialized direct-manipulation canvases.

Even then, surrounding text and controls should reflow normally.

---

# 18. Accessibility constitution

Accessibility is part of premium resolution.

## 18.1 Keyboard

- logical focus order;
- visible focus;
- skip links where useful;
- menu Escape;
- modal focus trap/release;
- focus restoration;
- no hover-only essential functions;
- no drag-only function without alternative when nonessential.

## 18.2 Target size

WCAG 2.2 minimum target-size criteria and spacing must be respected.

For important touch controls, use the stronger app-quality target around **44×44** when practical.

## 18.3 Reduced motion

Reduced motion is an **alternate composition**, not "everything at 0.01ms."

Replace:

- large spatial travel;
- zoom;
- repeated peripheral motion;
- z-axis shifts;
- heavy parallax

with:

- stable layout;
- short opacity;
- direct state change;
- non-spatial emphasis;
- static final state.

Do not destroy focus/state feedback.

## 18.4 Focus not obscured

Sticky headers, footers and overlays must not cover focused controls.

## 18.5 Meaning

Do not encode meaning only through:

- color;
- motion;
- pointer position;
- canvas;
- sound.

Provide semantic DOM/text alternatives for visualizations.

---

# 19. Performance constitution

Creative frontend work has no exemption from performance.

Internal quality targets:

- LCP ≤ 2.5s at p75;
- INP ≤ 200ms at p75;
- CLS ≤ 0.1 at p75.

Treat these as engineering targets, not marketing promises.

## 19.1 Images

- hero LCP image eager/high-priority;
- correct `srcset`/`sizes`;
- responsive art-direction sources;
- below-fold lazy;
- fixed intrinsic dimensions/aspect ratio;
- modern formats;
- do not preload the entire rail/gallery.

## 19.2 Video

- poster;
- appropriate preload;
- muted autoplay only when justified;
- no invisible video downloads without reason;
- mobile substitution where necessary;
- reduced-motion consideration.

## 19.3 Heavy experiences

If a 3D/media system fails or is too slow, preserve:

- semantic content;
- navigation;
- product understanding;
- conversion/action.

A fallback must be a designed version of the experience, not an apology screen.

## 19.4 Loader

A loader is justified only when essential assets truly require it.

Rules:

- no artificial minimum duration;
- no fake percentage;
- release as soon as the meaningful opening is ready;
- do not hide a slow implementation behind theatre;
- loader language should belong to brand only when the waiting state itself has value.

---

# 20. Copy and content design

Copy is interface.

## 20.1 Human, specific, restrained

Avoid:

- "transform";
- "elevate";
- "unlock";
- "revolutionize";
- "AI-powered";
- "seamless";
- "cutting-edge";
- "next-generation"

unless the specific sentence earns it.

Avoid repeated:

- three-part slogans;
- fake "not X, but Y";
- dramatic fragments;
- adjective stacking;
- em-dash dependency;
- vague CTAs.

## 20.2 Content follows visual evidence

The homepage should not explain everything.

Use detailed routes for:

- methodology;
- trust;
- privacy;
- technical details;
- full feature inventories;
- legal/retention;
- deeper product proof.

The homepage should establish:

- proposition;
- protagonist;
- core transformation;
- proof;
- next action.

## 20.3 Trust language

Never increase legal/security certainty merely to make the interface feel trustworthy.

If backend/policy evidence is unresolved, the copy must remain bounded.

---

# 21. Dashboard and product-app doctrine

Marketing can be cinematic.

Operational product UI should be task-first.

## 21.1 Hierarchy

A dashboard is not an inventory of cards.

Prioritize:

- dominant current task;
- attention state;
- recent work/history;
- exceptions;
- progress;
- secondary detail.

## 21.2 Maturity states

Design explicitly for:

- D0 — no data / no completed work;
- D1 — one result / one run;
- D2+ — longitudinal history.

Do not show "trends" when there is no trend.

## 21.3 Cards

Product cards are acceptable when they are real objects:

- assessment;
- simulation;
- delivery;
- order;
- report;
- alert;
- booking;
- saved model.

Avoid decorating every metric in its own floating rounded rectangle.

---

# 22. Data visualization

Every visualization answers a question.

Before drawing a chart, write the question.

Examples:

- What changed?
- What dominates?
- What is uncertain?
- Where does this role align?
- What is missing?
- Which input drove the result?
- How does this compare to the previous run?
- What needs attention?

Rules:

- neutral base;
- controlled accent;
- semantic color;
- no rainbow by category unless truly necessary;
- no decoration competing with data;
- uncertainty shown honestly;
- missing data absent/labeled, not invented;
- accessible text/table equivalent;
- useful tooltips;
- mobile alternative;
- no fake chart in marketing.

---

# 23. Research library — designer-brain reconstruction

The source corpus includes extensive direct/live and secondary research. The important transferable lessons are summarized here.

## 23.1 White Desert

Designer-brain lesson:

> preserve the world longer than the content.

Observed strengths:

- opening is a complete environment, not header + hero;
- grid persists;
- landscape changes while navigation remains integrated;
- vertical scene fractures into lateral camp sequence;
- incoming scene begins before outgoing scene disappears;
- wide environmental media establishes scale;
- facts arrive after emotional orientation;
- footer resolves the journey rather than ending design abruptly.

Transfer:

- world continuity;
- compositional handoff;
- semantic horizontal movement;
- media scale sequencing;
- integrated header/footer.

Do not copy:

- Antarctica;
- exact grid;
- camp card look;
- serif/condensed pairing;
- orange tab;
- ice palette.

## 23.2 Lando Norris

Designer-brain lesson:

> use brand-native identity actors, not generic motifs.

Observed:

- signature;
- helmet;
- personal/racing duality;
- large type;
- lifestyle/race artifact mix;
- On/Off Track portal;
- final helmet totem.

Transfer:

- recurring identity actor;
- duality as navigation;
- artifacts as proof;
- commercial content after identity;
- authored footer.

Do not copy:

- acid lime;
- helmet;
- racing language;
- scribble.

## 23.3 Outfit

Designer-brain lesson:

> brand continuity must survive from load to hover to product to bag.

Transfer:

- loader can establish identity when waiting is real;
- hover can be a sentence;
- alternate media reveals;
- transactional state can still feel authored;
- conversion should not become visually alien.

Do not copy:

- `000`;
- red/cream;
- exact cursor;
- wordmark.

## 23.4 Inversa

Designer-brain lesson:

> invisible operational complexity becomes understandable through named states.

Transfer:

- workflow as visual state machine;
- field/data/map/human evidence;
- reversible progression;
- density rises/falls;
- systems become scenes.

Do not copy:

- lime/black;
- body-cam/heatmap surfaces;
- ecology language.

## 23.5 Jasmine Gunarto

Designer-brain lesson:

> typography, project artifacts, metadata and pacing can make a portfolio feel like a publication.

Transfer:

- typography as structure;
- process/role/tools/credits;
- media scale rhythm;
- project-specific composition inside a shared system.

Do not copy:

- exact wordmark;
- condensed typography;
- project sequence.

## 23.6 Osmo

Designer-brain lesson:

> name interaction primitives and demonstrate capability rather than describing it.

Transfer:

- working previews;
- modular motion vocabulary;
- productized interaction knowledge;
- designed locked/unlocked states;
- reusable mechanics.

Do not copy:

- radial carousel;
- green marquee;
- resource card surfaces.

## 23.7 K95 / Igloo / WebGL failure lessons

Transfer:

- progressive enhancement;
- accessible project index;
- basic information must survive renderer failure;
- visual identity cannot depend on one fragile canvas.

## 23.8 Oryzo / Lusion

The 2026 Lusion behind-the-scenes series reinforces several core rules.

Their early "typical Awwwards" direction was clean and stylish but felt lifeless. The solution was not a more complex layout. They created a believable world around the product, kept the product central, prioritized continuity, used fewer UI ideas, and allowed a human hand-drawn layer to counterbalance technical polish.

Lusion's stated production principle is especially important:

> the pipeline follows the idea, not the other way around.

Transfer:

- concept first;
- protagonist first;
- visual world first;
- realistic/material evidence;
- seamless transitions;
- restraint;
- fewer competing UI ideas;
- human irregularity where appropriate.

Do not copy:

- coaster;
- AI satire;
- Apple parody;
- exact desk scene.

## 23.9 Vizcom / OFF+BRAND

The objective was to make the product understandable in the first few seconds.

The hero demonstrates:

- sketch;
- transform;
- iterate.

Transfer:

> demonstrate the product's native transformation before asking the visitor to read a feature list.

## 23.10 Podium

The team explicitly moved away from page-based portfolio structure because it broke the rhythm of the work.

The selected media becomes the page-transition object.

Transfer:

- continuous sequence when the subject earns it;
- media carries transition;
- restraint;
- rhythm;
- content-aligned motion.

## 23.11 Unseen Studio

Transfer:

- abstract/invisible processes can become explorable worlds;
- portfolio navigation can itself visualize information relationships;
- storytelling and practical discovery can coexist.

## 23.12 Lesse Studio

A critical counterweight:

Their previous site was visually experimental but important information was harder to find. Their newer direction sought clarity, direct navigation, intentional motion and lower technical overhead.

Transfer:

> art direction does not excuse making users work unnecessarily.

Concept and creative direction.

## R4 — Lusion Oryzo BTS Part 3
UX/UI and illustration.

Key refresh:

https://blog.lusion.co/oryzo-bts-part-3-7-website-ux-ui-and-illustrations

## R5 — OFF+BRAND / Vizcom
Key refresh:
- hero should make the product instantly understandable;
